Daytona Beach|United States of America.f: Malcolm Campbell set a 276.816 mph land speed record on the sand here in 1935, ending Daytona's land speed racing days.

Pueblo|United States of America.f: Pueblo is the hometown of four Medal of Honor recipients, tied with Holland, Michigan for the most of any US city.

Mesa|United States of America.f: By 1100 CE the Hohokam people here could water over 110,000 acres of Sonoran Desert with their irrigation canals.

Wichita|United States of America.f: Pizza Hut began in Wichita in 1958, and White Castle opened here in 1921.

Stockton|United States of America.f: The Caterpillar tractor got its name after a Holt photographer saw it crawl in a 1904 Stockton test and compared it to a caterpillar.

Melbourne (FL)|United States of America.f: Melbourne was named by its first postmaster, an Englishman who had spent much of his life in Melbourne, Australia.

Cold Bay|United States of America.f: Cold Bay's 10,180-foot runway began as WWII Fort Randall Army Airfield and now serves as a diversion point for transpacific flights.

Casper|United States of America.f: Casper is spelled differently from Fort Caspar and Lt. Caspar Collins, its namesakes, because of a typo at official registration.

Peoria|United States of America.f: The mold used to mass-produce penicillin was first isolated from a moldy cantaloupe found at a Peoria grocery store.

Meridian|United States of America.f: Meridian's Dentzel carousel, running since 1909, is the world's only two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie.

Moline|United States of America.f: John Deere moved his steel plow company to Moline, where Deere & Company still has its world headquarters, designed by Eero Saarinen.

Rock Springs|United States of America.f: In 1885 white miners killed their Chinese coworkers in the Rock Springs massacre, one of the worst anti-immigrant attacks in US history.

Atlantic City|United States of America.f: The first Atlantic City boardwalk was built in 1870 to help hotel owners keep sand out of their lobbies.

Harrisburg|United States of America.f: The Pennsylvania Farm Show, the largest indoor agriculture exposition in the US, has been held in Harrisburg every January since 1917.

Belleville|United States of America.f: Belleville takes its name from the French belle ville, meaning beautiful city.

Panama City (FL)|United States of Americ.f: The town of Harrison became Panama City because a line from Chicago to Panama's capital crosses it, a Canal-era land sales pitch.

Longview|United States of America.f: Construction of the Big Inch pipeline began in Longview in 1942, and it carried over 261 million barrels of crude east by 1945.

Steamboat Springs|United States of Ameri.f: Steamboat Springs has produced more Winter Olympics athletes than any other town in North America.

Montrose|United States of America.f: The Gunnison Tunnel east of Montrose opened in 1909 and was the world's longest irrigation tunnel at 5.8 miles.

Killeen|United States of America.f: Killeen was named for Frank P. Killeen, a railroad assistant general manager, when the railroad platted a 70-block town in 1881.

Hilo|United States of America.f: Hilo recorded 27.24 inches of rain in 24 hours on November 2, 2000.

Midland|United States of America.f: Midland started as Midway for its spot between Fort Worth and El Paso, and was renamed in 1884 because other Texas towns used Midway.

Missoula|United States of America.f: About 13,000 years ago the whole Missoula valley sat at the bottom of Glacial Lake Missoula.

Gunnison|United States of America.f: Gunnison's coldest recorded temperature was -47 F on December 25, 1924.

Harlingen|United States of America.f: Founder Lon C. Hill named Harlingen in 1904 after the Frisian city of Harlingen in the Netherlands.

Alexandria (LA)|United States of America.f: The Kent Plantation House is one of only two Alexandria buildings that survived the 1864 burning by retreating Union troops.

Grand Junction|United States of America.f: Grand Junction is named for the meeting of the Colorado and Gunnison rivers and the old Grand River, renamed the Colorado in 1921.

St George|United States of America.f: The St. George Utah Temple, completed in April 1877, is the oldest LDS temple still in active use.

Cheyenne|United States of America.f: Cheyenne grew so fast after its founding in 1867 that it earned the nickname Magic City of the Plains.

Manchester (NH)|United States of America.f: Manchester's Amoskeag Mill No. 11 was the world's largest cotton mill, 900 feet long with 4,000 looms.

Alliance|United States of America.f: Carhenge, a Stonehenge replica made of 38 vehicles, was built near Alliance by a family in the summer of 1987.

Durango|United States of America.f: Ex-Governor Alexander Hunt named Durango after Durango, Mexico, which he liked on a scouting trip for railroad founder William Palmer.

Victoria (TX)|United States of America.f: Victoria is named for Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of independent Mexico.

Marquette|United States of America.f: Marquette averages 149.1 inches of snow a year.

Pocatello|United States of America.f: Pocatello is named after Chief Pocatello, a 19th-century Northern Shoshone leader.

Rochester (MN)|United States of America.f: After an 1883 tornado killed 37 people in Rochester, the Mayo family's care of the wounded led to St. Marys Hospital in 1889.

Montgomery|United States of America.f: In 1886 Montgomery became the first US city with citywide electric streetcars, nicknamed the Lightning Route.

Kalispell|United States of America.f: Kalispell comes from a Salish word meaning flat land above the lake.

Madison|United States of America.f: Downtown Madison sits on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona, hence the phrase Lake, City, Lake.

Gulfport|United States of America.f: Gulfport got its name in 1888 from Jackson Clarion-Ledger editor R. H. Henry, after a conversation with founder William H. Hardy.
